The first bad use case is always the small one: a variable rename, a config tweak, a function that needs one extra argument. Gergő would hand a coding agent a task that should have taken thirty seconds, then watch it inspect half the repository, explain the architecture back to him, and occasionally decide the real problem was something adjacent. The tool was not broken. It was doing exactly what it had been built to do: expanding the search space.

That became the first useful boundary. Coding agents are not good or bad in the abstract. They are expensive in proportion to how unnecessary they are.

By "claw," he means the mode where you stop typing every line yourself and let an agent roam. It reads files, runs commands, edits code, and comes back with a patch. Sometimes that patch is excellent. Sometimes it is a theatrical performance of competence wrapped around a two-line fix you could have made before the agent finished loading context.

This is why the usual question about coding agents turns useless so quickly. "Are they good?" is too blunt to help. What matters is the shape of the work.

A good claw task has a certain texture. The repo is unfamiliar, or large enough that keeping the whole thing in your head would be annoying. The problem lives across seams. There is search involved, maybe a little archaeology, maybe a little glue work. You can describe what done looks like, but you do not want to personally walk through every boring step needed to get there. That is where the agent starts earning its keep.

He found it useful to separate coding work into three rough modes. Some tasks are conversational. You are still deciding what the thing should be. You want to talk through tradeoffs, sketch shapes, ask whether the abstraction is wrong, or figure out why an implementation feels ugly before touching the code. For that, he prefers staying in the editor with a tighter assistant like Pi. The point is not delegation. The point is thinking.

Some tasks are surgical. You already know the fix. You know the file. You probably know the line. In that case an agent is overhead. It has to load context, make inferences, and prove to itself that the problem is real. You just need to type the damn change and move on.

Claw lives in the middle: concrete enough to delegate, messy enough to be worth delegating. Rename this across the repo and make sure nothing breaks. Trace where this value enters the system and why it disappears two layers later. Wire a new field through the backend, API layer, and frontend. Read the docs, inspect the code, try the obvious fix, then tell me where the actual constraint is. These are not glamorous tasks. That is part of the point. Agents are often best at the work nobody wants to do carefully by hand.

This middle zone only made sense to him once his tool stack split into layers. Neovim used to be the precision instrument: the thing he reached for when he wanted exact control over every keystroke and every movement. Then Pi started absorbing some of that role. The reason was not magic. It was observability. Pi could be watched, interrupted, redirected. He could see the line of attack forming and step in before the agent wandered too far into the weeds.

What used to require a hyper-customized editor increasingly became a dialogue with a coding agent sitting closer to the code than a general chat assistant ever could. And then even Pi stopped being the first stop for everything. Once Cody existed as the always-on layer, conversation moved upward. Workflows, reminders, planning, lightweight scripting, rough problem-shaping: all of that could happen in the ongoing thread of daily life.

The practical stack became editor when precision matters, Pi when implementation gets swampy, Cody when the problem is still partly made of words. None of the layers killed the previous one. They changed what counted as worth reaching for. That threshold is the real subject here.

A second boundary appears around blast radius. Gergő came into agents from the paranoid side. Containers, wrappers, hard boundaries, minimal trust. That instinct transfers cleanly to coding agents. The right claw task is one where review is cheap and failure is survivable. If the agent makes a dumb edit, you want that to show up in a diff, not in a production database or a silently corrupted setup.

Delegation works best when the cleanup cost stays bounded. This is also why he does not like using agents for the most personal parts of a codebase. A tiny config he touches every day. A naming decision that sets the tone of a whole project. A piece of writing-heavy interface copy. Anything where the exact shape matters more than the mere existence of a working patch.

Agents can do these things. That is not the same as them being the right tool for them.

The token economics make the same point from another angle. A conversational agent carries context: memory, persona, old turns, accumulated preferences, the whole relationship. That is useful when the task depends on continuity. It is wasteful when the task is just code. A coding agent starts fresh. Give it the repo, the problem, the constraints, and let it work. For pure implementation, that statelessness is not a limitation. It is the reason the tool is efficient.

He once put it to me in a way that was slightly unfair but not wrong: a stateful assistant charges you for the relationship, while a coding agent charges you for the task.

That difference is why observability matters so much. Being able to watch an agent work is not just psychologically comforting. It changes the economics. If you can interrupt halfway through a bad approach, you save time, tokens, and cleanup. If the agent hides the path it is taking behind a sequence of conversational turns, course correction comes later and costs more. The more concrete the task, the more valuable that visibility becomes.

The temptation is to frame this as craft versus laziness. He does not think that is what is going on. The better distinction is between work that benefits from compression and work that benefits from contact. Some problems should be collapsed into a reviewed patch. Others need your hands on them because the point is not just to finish them. The point is to learn the terrain while you move through it.

That last part matters more than most agent demos admit. If you are using a task to understand a codebase, handing it off can be self-defeating. You get the answer without building the map. The same goes for bugs that carry a lesson. Sometimes the slow walk through the files is the value. The fix is almost incidental.

An agent can remove that friction. It can also remove the education.

This is where the more breathless stories about AI coding start to feel off. They treat all friction as waste. Gergő's experience has been narrower. Some friction is drag: search, glue code, repetitive edits, setup churn, mechanical migration work. Offload that. Some friction is signal: a stubborn function, an ugly interface boundary, a naming decision that refuses to settle. Those moments are often telling you something. If you claw too early, you skip the part where the problem explains itself.

So when should you claw? When the task spans files, tools, or layers. When the acceptance criteria are clear enough to review. When the work is annoying in a mechanical way. When you are happy to evaluate a diff instead of experiencing every keystroke. When failure will be visible and reversible.

When should you not? When the task is tiny. When the task is the lesson. When the code is delicate in a way the diff will not capture. When you care about taste more than throughput. When you already know exactly what to do and the agent would just be an expensive middleman.

He still uses coding agents a lot. Probably more than he would have predicted a year ago. But the mature version of the habit looks less like surrendering the keyboard and more like choosing where autonomy belongs. Delegate the swamp. Keep the knife work. Stay close to anything you might want to understand later.

That, at least, is the current rule. It will probably change again.
